figureFiles.caption: The lung and the two main groups of air sacs, with structures labeled in the left panel. Fresh air (blue) reaches the lung from the caudal sacs and used air (orange) leaves by way of the cranial sacs, so the flow through the parabronchi (green) runs from back to front during both inhalation and exhalation.

The path of food in a seed-eating bird such as a pigeon. Storage (crop), chemical digestion (proventriculus) and grinding (gizzard) all happen before the intestine; the ceca are side pouches (tiny in pigeons, large in plant-eaters such as grouse), and the cloaca is the shared exit.

Cone pigments of a human and of a Blue Tit, drawn with a standard pigment-absorbance template at approximate measured peaks. The bird’s fourth cone reaches into the ultraviolet, which the human lens blocks; in birds, colored oil droplets narrow each cone’s range more than these pigment curves show.

lesson.hook: Every spring, Bar-headed Geese (*Anser indicus*) that spend the winter on lakes and rivers in lowland India set off for breeding grounds in Central Asia, and the Himalayas stand in the way. When researchers fitted geese with GPS tags, they found that some birds crossed the range in a single day, typically climbing 4,000 to 6,000 meters in 7 to 8 hours. The highest reading came from one goose flying briefly at 7,290 meters. Mountaineers once reported geese passing high overhead, and the story grew that they fly over the summit of Everest; tracking has never shown that, because the birds mostly follow valleys and passes. Even so, at 5,500 meters each breath holds about half the oxygen it would at sea level, and the goose is flapping the whole way. The explanation lies inside the bird.
lesson.overview: Chapter 1 showed you the outside of a bird and its skeleton, and Chapter 2 showed how much energy flight demands. This chapter opens the body. You will see how air sacs drive air through the lungs in one direction, why birds run hot and how some of them deliberately cool down at night, how an animal with no teeth digests seeds and leaves, and how bird senses compare with ours, from color vision that reaches into the ultraviolet to the vultures and seabirds that find food by smell. Each system serves the same high-energy way of life. The ideas return in Chapter 5, where air moving through the syrinx makes song, and in Chapter 7, where fuel stores and the senses carry migrants across oceans.
objectives: Trace the path of air through a bird’s air sacs and lungs and explain why the flow through the gas-exchange tubes is one-way.
Explain how birds keep a high body temperature, what it costs, and how torpor saves energy.
Describe the jobs of the crop, proventriculus and gizzard, and relate the design of the gut to diet.
Compare bird and human color vision, and name birds that find food by sound or by smell.

sections.title: Breathing with air sacs
reading: As Chapter 2 showed, flapping flight is one of the most expensive things a vertebrate body can do, and every bit of that energy is released by burning fuel with oxygen. Your own lungs collect oxygen in a surprisingly wasteful way. Air travels down branching tubes into hundreds of millions of dead-end pockets, the alveoli, then comes back out the way it went in. Each new breath mixes with stale air left behind, so the air touching your blood is never fully fresh. Birds use a different design. Their lungs are small, stiff and fixed against the ribs, and they barely change volume. The pumping is done by a set of thin-walled **air sacs**, usually about nine of them, which fill much of the body cavity and in many species extend into the hollow bones you met in Chapter 1 [1].

The air sacs work like bellows. They have few blood vessels and take almost no part in gas exchange [1]. Birds have no diaphragm. Instead, muscles swing the sternum and ribs down and forward to breathe in, enlarging the body cavity so the sacs expand, and draw them back to breathe out. The sacs fall into two groups: the **caudal air sacs** toward the rear of the body and the **cranial air sacs** toward the front. Between them lies the lung, threaded by many narrow, parallel tubes called **parabronchi**. From the wall of each parabronchus runs a dense network of tiny **air capillaries**, wound together with blood capillaries. This is where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it [1].

Follow the air through a Rock Pigeon (*Columba livia*) in Figure 3.1. When the bird breathes in, most of the fresh air rushes down the trachea and the main bronchus, straight past the lung and into the caudal sacs; some enters the parabronchi directly. At the same moment, air that was already in the lung moves forward into the cranial sacs. When the bird breathes out, the caudal sacs squeeze their fresh air into the lung, and the cranial sacs empty their used air out through the trachea. The result is that air crosses the parabronchi in the same direction, from back to front, during both inhalation and exhalation. The lung is bathed in a nearly continuous stream of fresh air instead of a tide that comes and goes [1, 2].

Finding out which way air moves inside a living bird took new instruments. In 1971, William Bretz and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen at Duke University built small probes that register the direction of airflow and placed them at different points in the airways of ducks. During normal breathing, the readings showed the one-way pattern through the main gas-exchange tubes [2]. Tracer-gas experiments that followed led to a popular summary: a single breath of air needs two full breathing cycles to pass through, into the caudal sacs on the first inhalation, through the lung on the first exhalation, into the cranial sacs on the second inhalation and out on the second exhalation [1]. Treat this as an average route, not a strict queue, because inhaled air spreads and mixes along the way. Anatomists have searched for valves that could enforce the one-way flow and found none. The steering appears to come from the shape of the airway junctions and the momentum of the moving air, a mechanism called **aerodynamic valving** [1].

The design has a second advantage. In the parabronchi, blood capillaries run across the air stream rather than alongside it, an arrangement called **cross-current exchange**. Blood leaving the lung has met the air at many points along the tube, so it can end up richer in oxygen than the air the bird breathes out, something a mammal lung cannot achieve [1, 5]. That edge matters most where oxygen is scarce. The Bar-headed Goose adds its own refinements to the general bird plan. Compared with lowland geese, it breathes more deeply in thin air, its hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly, and its flight muscles are richer in capillaries, so oxygen moves more easily at each step from the air to the muscle cells [5].

This breathing system is older than birds. In 2010, C. G. Farmer and Kent Sanders measured airflow in the lungs of American Alligators (*Alligator mississippiensis*), which have no air sacs, and found that air also moves one way through their lungs. The pattern persisted in lungs removed from the body, so it comes from the structure of the airways themselves [3]. Crocodilians and birds are the two living branches of the archosaurs, so one-way airflow probably goes back to their common ancestor in the Triassic. Fossils supply the next piece. The vertebrae of the theropod dinosaur *Majungasaurus*, about 67 million years old, from Madagascar, carry openings in the same pattern that air sacs leave in the bones of living birds. This is evidence that bird-style air sacs were already present in non-avian theropods [4].

keyTerms.def: A thin-walled, balloon-like chamber connected to the lungs that pumps air but does little or no gas exchange.
One of the many narrow, parallel tubes running through a bird’s lung, along whose walls gas exchange takes place.
One of the tiny air passages branching from a parabronchus and wound together with blood capillaries.
Air moving through the gas-exchange tubes in the same direction during both inhalation and exhalation.
An arrangement in which blood capillaries cross the air stream at many points, letting blood pick up oxygen efficiently.
The steering of airflow by the shape of airway junctions and the momentum of the air, without any physical valves.

example.title: Worked example: following one breath through a Rock Pigeon
steps: First inhalation: the pigeon’s sternum swings down and forward, the air sacs expand, and fresh air rushes down the trachea. Most of it passes along the main bronchus, past the lung, into the caudal air sacs.

First exhalation: the sternum moves back, the caudal sacs are squeezed, and their fresh air is pushed forward through the parabronchi. Oxygen crosses into the blood in the air capillaries, and carbon dioxide moves out.
Second inhalation: this now-used air moves on, out of the lung and into the cranial air sacs, while a new breath fills the caudal sacs behind it.
Second exhalation: the cranial sacs empty, and the used air leaves through the trachea.
Check the direction: in the first exhalation and the second inhalation the air crossed the parabronchi from back to front both times. That is the one-way flow.
example.takeaway: The air sacs pump and the lung exchanges gas; separating the two jobs lets fresh air cross the exchange surface in one direction during both phases of breathing.

misconception.myth: Birds breathe in and out of their lungs just like we do, only faster.
misconception.fact: A bird’s lungs barely change volume. The air sacs do the pumping, and air flows one way through the parabronchi during both inhalation and exhalation. In mammals, air moves in and out of the same dead-end alveoli and mixes with stale air.

practice.q: Which structures exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood in a bird?
choices: The air capillaries around the parabronchi
practice.explanation: Gas exchange happens in the air capillaries that branch from the parabronchi. The air sacs have few blood vessels and act as bellows, the hollow bones are air-filled extensions of the sacs, and the trachea only carries air.

practice.q: A wildlife rehabilitator is handling an injured pigeon. Using this section, explain why holding the bird too tightly around the body could stop it breathing, even if its head and beak are free.
practice.answer: Birds have no diaphragm. They breathe by moving the sternum and ribs down and forward, which expands the body cavity so the air sacs fill, and then back again to empty them. A tight grip around the body stops those movements, so the air sacs cannot pump air through the lungs, even though the airway is open.
practice.explanation: A good answer says that the air sacs, driven by movements of the sternum and ribs, do the pumping, and that birds lack a diaphragm, so restraining the body wall blocks breathing.

practice.q: Lungs removed from an alligator are ventilated with a pump, and air still flows one way through their tubes. What does this result show?
choices: One-way flow comes from the structure of the airways themselves
The flow is produced by the diaphragm
practice.explanation: The lungs were outside the body, with no air sacs, muscles or diaphragm attached, yet the flow was still one-way. So the arrangement of the airways must produce it. Alligators are archosaurs, close relatives of birds, but not birds.

sections.title: Metabolism and body temperature
reading: Birds are **endotherms**: like mammals, they make most of their body heat internally by burning food, and they hold a steady core temperature whatever the weather. They run hotter than we do. Most birds keep their core between about 38 and 42 °C, usually a little higher during the active part of the day than at rest, compared with about 37 °C in a human [1]. A warm body has faster chemistry, so muscles contract quickly and nerves fire fast, which helps an animal that must react in flight. The cost is fuel. A bird’s **metabolic rate**, the rate at which it uses energy, is high even at rest and climbs steeply when it flies [1].

Measuring that cost takes ingenuity. The standard method is to measure how much oxygen an animal uses, because each liter of oxygen consumed corresponds to a known amount of energy released. In 2019, Jessica Meir and colleagues raised Bar-headed Geese by hand from hatching, so that the birds imprinted on people, and trained them to fly in a wind tunnel while wearing masks that sampled their breath. In flight, the geese used energy about 16 times faster than at rest, and the extra oxygen was delivered mainly by more oxygen per heartbeat, with only a modest rise in heart rate [4]. The team then lowered the oxygen in the air to match altitudes of 5,500 and 9,000 meters. In thin air the geese’s metabolic rate in flight fell below its level in normal air, and their heart rate did not climb any higher [4].

Wild birds face the same budget. GPS tracking showed that Bar-headed Geese from lowland India can cross the Himalayas in a single day, typically climbing 4,000 to 6,000 meters in 7 to 8 hours, and that they tended to avoid the strong winds of the afternoon, climbing even in the still air of night [2]. A later study implanted loggers that recorded heart rate, a stand-in for energy use, along with altitude. Flight cost rose quickly as the air thinned, so the geese followed the terrain, dropping into valleys and climbing again rather than holding a high altitude. In that study the geese spent most of their flight time below 6,000 meters, and the highest single record was a brief 7,290 meters [3]. The circulation behind this effort resembles ours in one way: birds have a four-chambered heart that keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood fully apart. Bird hearts are also, on average, larger for their body size than mammal hearts [1].

Body size changes the budget. A small body has more surface for each gram of tissue, so it loses heat faster, and small birds must burn energy faster per gram to stay warm. Hummingbirds sit at the extreme: for their weight, hovering hummingbirds have some of the highest metabolic rates measured in any vertebrate [1]. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird (*Archilochus colubris*) weighs about 3 grams, and by day it refuels with nectar and small insects many times an hour. A long, cool night without food is therefore a real danger, because the bird’s small fat store could run out before dawn [1].

The solution is **torpor**, a controlled drop in body temperature and metabolic rate. On a cold night a hummingbird can let its body temperature fall far below its daytime level and cut its energy use sharply, then rewarm by shivering before it starts feeding again [1]. The record holders are hummingbirds of the high Andes. In 2020, Blair Wolf and colleagues recorded a Black Metaltail (*Metallura phoebe*) whose body temperature fell to about 3.3 °C during torpor, the lowest yet measured in a bird [5]. One bird goes further still. In the 1940s the naturalist Edmund Jaeger found a Common Poorwill (*Phalaenoptilus nuttallii*) in a rock crevice in the California desert, cold and motionless, and it stayed torpid for weeks. The poorwill is still the only bird known to spend long stretches of the winter in a state close to hibernation [1].

Holding a steady temperature also means getting rid of heat. Feathers are excellent insulation, and a cold bird fluffs them to trap more air and shivers to make heat. A hot bird does the reverse. Birds have no sweat glands, so they lose heat by evaporating water from the mouth and airways, either by panting or by rapidly vibrating the throat, a behavior called **gular fluttering** [1]. Legs and feet pose their own problem, because they are thin and bare. In many birds, warm arteries running down the leg lie against cold veins coming back up, so heat passes from one to the other before it reaches the foot. This **countercurrent heat exchange** lets a gull stand on ice with cold feet while its core stays warm [1].

keyTerms.def: An animal that produces most of its body heat internally and keeps a steady core temperature, as birds and mammals do.
The rate at which an animal uses energy, usually measured from the oxygen it consumes.
A controlled drop in body temperature and metabolic rate that saves energy, lasting hours or, in the Common Poorwill, weeks.
Rapid vibration of the throat that evaporates water and cools a hot bird.
Heat passing from warm outgoing blood to cold returning blood in vessels that lie side by side, which keeps heat in the body core.

example.title: Worked example: why a hummingbird needs torpor and a goose does not
steps: Compare sizes. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird weighs about 3 grams; a Bar-headed Goose weighs several hundred times as much.
Apply the size rule. If one body is 10 times longer than another of the same shape, it has 100 times the surface area but 1,000 times the mass, so it has only one-tenth as much surface for each gram.
So the hummingbird has far more surface per gram than the goose. It loses heat much faster for its weight and must burn fuel much faster per gram to stay near 40 °C.

Overnight the hummingbird cannot feed. Heat loss depends on the difference between body and air temperature, so by letting its body cool in torpor it cuts that difference and saves much of its small fat store.
The goose, with little surface per gram and large reserves, can keep its normal temperature through a cold night without torpor.
example.takeaway: Small bodies lose heat fastest for their weight, which is why the smallest birds are the ones that rely most on torpor.

misconception.myth: A hummingbird found cold, fluffed up and unresponsive on a chilly morning must be dying.
misconception.fact: It is very likely in torpor, a normal energy-saving state. Its body temperature and metabolism have been turned down for the night, and it will rewarm by shivering and fly off. The best help is usually to leave it alone.

choices: A controlled lowering of body temperature and metabolic rate that saves energy
A fever that helps a bird fight infection
Ordinary sleep with no change in body temperature
The loss of feathers during cold weather
practice.explanation: Torpor is a regulated drop in body temperature and metabolism. It is not a fever (which raises temperature), not ordinary sleep (in which temperature drops only a little), and has nothing to do with molt.

practice.q: A 10-gram songbird and a 1-kilogram duck spend the same night in air at −10 °C. Which bird faces the larger energy problem for each gram of its body, and what are two things a small bird could do to reduce that problem?
practice.answer: The songbird. It has far more surface area per gram, so it loses heat faster for its weight and must burn fuel faster per gram to stay warm. It could fluff its feathers to trap more insulating air, shelter in a cavity or dense cover out of the wind, or let its body temperature drop somewhat at night to reduce heat loss.
practice.explanation: A good answer uses the surface-to-mass reasoning from this section and gives two realistic responses, such as fluffing feathers, choosing a sheltered roost or lowering body temperature at night.

practice.q: In the wind-tunnel experiments by Meir and colleagues, what happened when Bar-headed Geese flew in air with its oxygen reduced to match high altitude?
choices: Their metabolic rate rose to record levels
Their metabolic rate in flight fell below its level in normal air, and their heart rate did not rise
They could not fly at all
practice.explanation: The geese flew in air matching 5,500 and 9,000 meters. Their metabolic rate in flight was lower than in normal air, and heart rate was no higher, which suggests they cope partly by reducing the energy cost of flight.

sections.title: Beaks, crops and gizzards
reading: In Chapter 1 you saw that birds have no teeth: a keratin beak covers the jaws, and its shape is adapted to the diet. A beak can crack, tear, probe, filter or spear, but it cannot chew. Most birds swallow food whole or in pieces, and the processing that a mammal does in its mouth happens further down the digestive tract [1]. An American Robin (*Turdus migratorius*) that tugs an earthworm from a lawn swallows it whole. In autumn and winter, when worms are harder to reach, robins eat far more fruit, and they swallow berries whole too [1]. Figure 3.2 follows food from beak to cloaca.

The first stop is the **esophagus**, a stretchy tube from mouth to stomach. In many birds, including pigeons, gamebirds, parrots, some finches, and hawks, eagles and falcons (but not owls), part of it is widened into a pouch called the **crop**. The crop is a storage bin. A pigeon on a busy sidewalk can fill its crop quickly and digest the meal later in safety, and you can sometimes see the bulge at the base of a well-fed pigeon’s neck. Not every bird has a crop, and in some it is only a slight widening [1]. In our Rock Pigeon the crop has a second use. Both parents produce **crop milk**, a rich secretion made of fat- and protein-filled cells shed from the crop lining, and feed it to their young [1].

Birds have a two-part stomach. The front part, the **proventriculus**, is glandular: it secretes acid and digestive enzymes that begin to break food down chemically. Food then passes to the **gizzard**, or ventriculus, a muscular grinding chamber with a tough, hard lining. In seed-eaters such as pigeons and sparrows the gizzard walls are thick and powerful, and the bird swallows small stones, called **grit**, which help crush hard seeds the way molars would. In birds that eat soft food such as fish, nectar or ripe fruit, the gizzard is thinner and less muscular [1]. Owls show what the gizzard can sort. They swallow small mammals whole, digest the flesh and cough up compact **pellets** of fur and bone, which researchers pull apart to learn exactly what an owl has eaten [1].

Diet can reshape the whole system. The Hoatzin (*Opisthocomus hoazin*) of South American river forests eats mostly leaves, a food few birds can use because plant cell walls are made of tough cellulose. In 1989, Alejandro Grajal and colleagues showed that the Hoatzin ferments leaves with bacteria in its enlarged crop and lower esophagus, the same strategy a cow uses in its rumen; it was the first bird known to digest food this way [2]. Grit in the gizzard has a long history. Fossils of the small feathered dinosaur *Caudipteryx*, described in 1998, preserve clusters of stones in the stomach region, much like the grit of plant-eating birds today. The stones suggest that some of these dinosaurs, like many birds today, ground their food in a muscular gizzard [3].

After the gizzard, food moves into the **small intestine**, where enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver finish digestion and nutrients are absorbed into the blood. Many birds have a pair of blind side pouches, the **ceca**, where the small and large intestines meet. They are largest in plant-eaters such as grouse, where bacteria inside them ferment tough plant fiber [1]. The large intestine is short and ends in the **cloaca**, a single chamber that also receives the outputs of the kidneys and the reproductive tract. Birds excrete nitrogen waste mainly as **uric acid**, which needs little water to flush away; it is the white part of a bird dropping, and the dark part is feces [1]. Fruit-eating birds pass seeds through quickly and drop them far from the parent plant, which makes them important seed dispersers [1].

The gut can also change size. Organs are heavy, and a flying bird pays to carry every gram. Theunis Piersma and Robert Gill examined Bar-tailed Godwits (*Limosa lapponica*) that had died in Alaska, probably just after setting off on their nonstop flight across the Pacific to New Zealand, a journey you will study in Chapter 7. The birds carried huge fat stores, but their digestive organs, including the gizzard and intestines, were unusually small for birds of their size [4]. Piersma and Gill concluded that the godwits had shrunk organs they would not use during the flight, trading digestive capacity for a lighter load. They titled their 1998 paper “Guts don’t fly” [4].

keyTerms.def: A pouch in the esophagus of many birds that stores food before digestion.
The glandular front part of a bird’s stomach, which secretes acid and digestive enzymes.
The muscular rear part of a bird’s stomach, which grinds food, often with the help of swallowed grit.
A pair of blind pouches where the small and large intestines meet, used for fermentation in many plant-eating birds.
The single chamber into which the digestive, urinary and reproductive tracts empty.
The main nitrogen waste of birds, excreted as a white paste that needs little water.

example.title: Worked example: following a grain of wheat through a Rock Pigeon
steps: Beak: the pigeon picks up the grain and swallows it whole. It has no teeth to crack it.
Crop: the grain waits in the crop with the rest of the meal while the pigeon keeps feeding. The bulge may show at the base of the neck.
Proventriculus: as the grain passes, glands coat it with acid and digestive enzymes.

Gizzard: thick muscles squeeze the grain against swallowed grit until the hard husk cracks and the contents are ground to a paste. Food can pass back and forth between gizzard and proventriculus, mixing grinding with chemical attack.
Intestine and cloaca: nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, and the remains reach the cloaca, where they leave with the white uric acid from the kidneys.
example.takeaway: Each part of the tract takes over a job that teeth would do in a mammal: storing, chemical attack, grinding and absorbing.

misconception.myth: Pigeons and chickens pecking at gravel are just picking it up by mistake.
misconception.fact: Many seed-eating birds swallow grit on purpose. The stones stay in the gizzard and help grind hard seeds, doing the job that teeth do in a mammal.

practice.q: Which organ in a pigeon grinds hard seeds?
practice.explanation: The gizzard is the muscular stomach that grinds food with the help of grit. The crop stores food, the proventriculus secretes acid and enzymes, and the cloaca is the shared exit.

practice.q: A museum preparator opens two birds. One has a thick, muscular gizzard containing small stones; the other has a thin-walled gizzard with no stones and the remains of small fish. One is a Mourning Dove and the other a Belted Kingfisher. Which is which, and why?
practice.answer: The thick gizzard with grit belongs to the Mourning Dove, a seed-eater that needs strong grinding to crack hard seeds. The thin gizzard with fish remains belongs to the Belted Kingfisher, which eats soft fish that acid and enzymes can break down without heavy grinding.
practice.explanation: A good answer matches the gizzard to the diet and explains that hard seeds need muscle and grit while soft animal food does not.

practice.q: What is the white part of a bird dropping?
practice.explanation: Birds excrete nitrogen waste as uric acid, which forms the white paste. It enters the cloaca from the kidneys and leaves together with the dark feces.

sections.title: Senses: vision, hearing and smell
reading: Birds are visual animals. Their eyes are very large for their heads; in many species the two eyes nearly meet in the middle of the skull, and an owl’s tube-shaped eyes can barely move in their sockets, which is why an owl turns its whole head to look around [1]. The retina at the back of the eye is packed with light-sensing cells. **Rods** work in dim light. **Cones** work in bright light and detect color. Many birds have a **fovea**, a small pit where cones are packed most densely and vision is sharpest, and hawks, eagles and some other birds that judge distance at speed have two foveae in each eye [1].

Human color vision rests on three types of cone, most sensitive to violet-blue, green and yellow-green light. Most birds have four types of single cone, so their color vision is **tetrachromatic**. The fourth type is sensitive to violet or **ultraviolet** light, wavelengths shorter than about 400 nanometers that we cannot see (Figure 3.3). In many songbirds and parrots this cone is most sensitive well into the ultraviolet; in others, such as chickens and most birds of prey, it peaks in the violet but still reaches into the ultraviolet. Most cones also hold a droplet of oil, usually colored, that filters light before it reaches the pigment, narrowing the range each cone responds to and sharpening color discrimination. Birds have **double cones** as well, thought to be used for judging brightness and motion rather than color [2].

These facts come from a technique called **microspectrophotometry**. Researchers pass a tiny beam of light, one wavelength at a time, through a single cone cell from a bird’s retina and measure which wavelengths its pigment absorbs [2]. Feathers tell the same story from the other side. Many plumages that look plain to us reflect strongly in the ultraviolet. The crown of the Blue Tit (*Cyanistes caeruleus*) of Europe looks blue to us, but instruments show that it also reflects ultraviolet light, and males and females, which look alike to a human observer, differ in that reflectance [2].

Hearing matters too, above all for song, the subject of Chapter 5. Most birds hear best between about 1 and 4 kilohertz, roughly the range of their songs, and few hear much above 10 kilohertz, while a young human can hear up to about 20 kilohertz [1]. Our running example uses its ears on the lawn. An American Robin hunting worms runs, stops and cocks its head. Because a robin’s eyes face sideways, the tilt was long read as looking. In experiments with captive robins, Robert Montgomerie and Patrick Weatherhead hid mealworms just under the soil surface and controlled which cues the birds could use. The robins still found prey when sound was the main cue available, evidence that they can hunt by ear as well as by eye [3].

The Barn Owl (*Tyto alba*) is the champion listener. In experiments published in 1971, Roger Payne showed that Barn Owls could catch mice in a light-tight room, and that they would strike at a wad of paper dragged across the floor, which ruled out sight, body heat and smell as the cues [4]. A Barn Owl’s ear openings sit at different heights on the two sides of its head, so a sound from below reaches one ear slightly differently than the other, and the dish-shaped disc of feathers around the face funnels sound toward the ears. Together these let the owl pinpoint prey both left to right and up and down in darkness [4].

Smell was long thought to matter little to birds; in the 1800s John James Audubon concluded from experiments that vultures found carrion by sight [1]. We now know that many birds smell well. The Turkey Vulture (*Cathartes aura*) has a large olfactory bulb and finds carcasses hidden under forest canopy by their odor. Pipeline workers have even located gas leaks by watching where Turkey Vultures gathered, because the gas carried an added odorant similar to the smell of decay [1]. Kiwis, alone among birds, have nostrils at the tip of the bill and sniff out worms in the soil [1]. At sea, many **tubenoses**, the group that includes albatrosses, petrels and shearwaters, can smell dimethyl sulfide, and some, such as storm-petrels and prions, are strongly drawn to it; the compound is released when krill and other small animals graze on plankton, so it leads the birds to rich feeding areas [5].

keyTerms.def: A light-sensing cell in the retina that works in bright light and contributes to color vision.
Color vision based on four types of cone, as in most birds; humans have three.
A small pit in the retina where cones are densest and vision is sharpest.
A droplet of oil, usually colored, inside a bird cone that filters light and narrows the range of wavelengths the cone responds to.
A technique that measures which wavelengths of light are absorbed by a single photoreceptor cell.
Albatrosses, petrels, shearwaters and their relatives, seabirds with tube-shaped nostrils and a keen sense of smell.

example.title: Worked example: reading a robin’s hunt on a lawn
steps: Watch an American Robin on short grass. It runs a few steps, stops, stands upright and tilts its head toward the ground, then sometimes lunges and pulls up a worm.
List the senses that could be at work: sight (its eyes face sideways, so a tilt aims one eye at the ground), hearing (a moving worm makes faint sounds), touch through the feet, and smell.
Check the evidence. Controlled experiments show that robins can find buried prey when sound is the main cue, and they clearly use sight to spot worms at the surface.
Conclude carefully. A head tilt could serve the eye, the ear or both, and watching alone cannot tell which. That is why researchers remove one cue at a time in experiments.
example.takeaway: Five minutes of watching a common bird raises questions about the senses that only controlled experiments can settle.

misconception.myth: Birds have almost no sense of smell.
misconception.fact: Many birds smell well. Turkey Vultures find hidden carcasses by odor, kiwis sniff for worms through nostrils at the tip of the bill, and many tubenoses track the smell of dimethyl sulfide across the ocean. The old view rested on a few early experiments and on studying mainly songbirds.

practice.q: Why can many birds see patterns on feathers and flowers that humans cannot?
choices: They have a fourth cone type sensitive to violet or ultraviolet light
Their eyes are larger than ours
They have more rods than we do
practice.explanation: The fourth single cone extends bird vision into the violet or ultraviolet, and the human lens blocks most ultraviolet light. Eye size and rods affect sharpness and night vision, not the range of colors, and birds do not see infrared.

practice.q: Design a simple field experiment to test whether Turkey Vultures find carcasses by smell rather than by sight.
practice.answer: Set out matched carcasses at several sites. Hide half of them completely under brush so they cannot be seen from the air, and leave the other half in view. As an extra test, put out odorless models that look like carcasses. Record how many of each type vultures find and how fast. If hidden carcasses are found about as often as visible ones and the odorless models are ignored, smell is the main cue.
practice.explanation: A strong answer separates the two cues (hidden but smelly versus visible but odorless), uses several replicates, and states what result would support the smell hypothesis.

practice.q: Two Blue Tits look identical to you, but one is a male and one a female. Which tool would best reveal a difference that the birds themselves can probably see?
choices: A spectrometer that measures ultraviolet reflectance
practice.explanation: Blue Tit crowns reflect ultraviolet light, and males and females differ in that reflectance. Birds see ultraviolet; we need an instrument to measure it.

interactives.title: Follow one breath through the air sacs
interactives.intro: Put the steps in order for a single breath of fresh air, from the moment it enters the trachea until it leaves again. Use Figure 3.1 if you get stuck.
steps: First inhalation: fresh air flows down the trachea and the main bronchus
Most of it passes the lung and fills the caudal air sacs
First exhalation: the caudal sacs push it forward through the parabronchi, where gas exchange happens
Second inhalation: the now-used air moves out of the lung into the cranial air sacs
Second exhalation: the cranial sacs empty and the air leaves through the trachea
interactives.explain: This is the two-cycle summary drawn from airflow and tracer-gas experiments on ducks. Real breaths mix and overlap, but the direction of flow through the parabronchi, from back to front, holds during both inhalation and exhalation.

interactives.title: How high birds have been recorded
interactives.intro: Air pressure, and with it the oxygen in each breath, falls with height: at 5,500 meters it is about half that at sea level. Compare where tracked Bar-headed Geese actually fly with the heights in popular stories.

items.label: Most Bar-headed Goose fixes
items.note: Among 91 tracked geese, 95 percent of locations were below this height; the birds mostly follow valleys and passes.

items.label: Highest goose record, northbound
items.note: From the same tracking study, on spring migration.

items.label: Highest goose record overall
items.note: One bird, briefly, on southbound migration.

items.label: Summit of Mount Everest
items.note: Tracking has never recorded a goose this high.

items.label: Wind-tunnel flight at simulated altitude
items.note: Captive geese flew in air with 7 percent oxygen, matching about 9,000 meters.

items.label: Rüppell’s Vulture struck by an airliner
items.note: Over Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, in November 1973, at about 37,000 feet; identified from feathers. The highest altitude recorded for a bird.

interactives.title: Which part of the gut does this job?
interactives.intro: Sort each job into the part of the digestive tract that does it. Figure 3.2 shows where each part sits.

items.text: Stores a quick meal for digestion later
items.why: The crop is a pouch in the esophagus that holds food while the bird keeps feeding.

items.text: Makes the “milk” fed to pigeon chicks
items.why: Both pigeon parents shed fat- and protein-rich cells from the crop lining to feed their young.

items.text: Ferments leaves with bacteria in the Hoatzin
items.why: The Hoatzin’s enlarged crop and lower esophagus work like a cow’s rumen.
The proventriculus is the glandular front part of the stomach.
The gizzard’s thick muscles and grit do the work of teeth.

items.text: Packs fur and bone into an owl pellet
items.why: Indigestible parts are held back and compacted in the gizzard, then coughed up.

items.text: Receives uric acid from the kidneys
items.why: The kidneys empty into the cloaca, so the white uric acid leaves with the feces.

items.text: Shared exit for the digestive, urinary and reproductive tracts
items.why: Cloaca is Latin for sewer: one chamber serves all three systems.

interactives.title: Do vultures hunt by smell?
interactives.intro: In the 1800s, John James Audubon concluded from experiments that vultures find carrion by sight. Later, pipeline workers noticed Turkey Vultures gathering over leaks in gas lines, where the gas carried an odorant that smells like decay. Work through the evidence as an ornithologist would.

steps.q: What do vultures gathering over a gas leak suggest, and why is it not yet proof?
steps.a: It suggests that Turkey Vultures are drawn by the smell of the odorant. But other explanations are possible: animals killed by the gas might be lying nearby, or the vultures might be following one another. An observation like this raises a hypothesis; it does not test it.

steps.q: How could you separate smell from sight in a field test?
steps.a: Hide some carcasses completely under vegetation so they cannot be seen from above, leave others in plain view, and add odorless look-alike models. If hidden carcasses are found and odorless models are ignored, smell is doing the work.

steps.q: Black Vultures often arrive at a carcass after Turkey Vultures have found it. What might explain this?
steps.a: Black Vultures rely more on sight and can watch for Turkey Vultures dropping down to food, then follow them. One species uses smell to find the food and the other uses sight to find the first species.

steps.q: Which other birds would you predict to have a strong sense of smell, given how they live?
steps.a: Birds that search for food that is hard to see: tubenoses over the open ocean, which follow the odor of dimethyl sulfide to feeding areas, and kiwis, which forage at night for worms in the soil with nostrils at the tip of the bill.

slides.title: Chapter 3: Inside the bird
bullets: Breathing with air sacs
Metabolism and body temperature
Beaks, crops and gizzards
Senses: vision, hearing and smell
slides.notes: Chapter 1 gave us the outside of the bird and Chapter 2 the demands of flight. Today we open the body and see how it pays for a high-energy life.

slides.title: The puzzle: flying through thin air
bullets: Bar-headed Geese can cross the Himalayas in a single day
Typical climb: 4,000 to 6,000 m in 7 to 8 hours
Highest record: a brief 7,290 m; not over Everest
At 5,500 m each breath holds about half the oxygen of a sea-level breath
slides.notes: Keep this goose in mind all chapter. By the end you should be able to explain each step that gets oxygen from the thin air into its flight muscles.

slides.title: Air sacs pump, lungs exchange
bullets: Lungs are small and rigid; about nine air sacs act as bellows
No diaphragm: the sternum and ribs move
Gas exchange in air capillaries around the parabronchi
Cross-current exchange extracts oxygen efficiently
slides.notes: Use Figure 3.1. The key idea is that the jobs are split: the sacs move air and the lung exchanges gas.

slides.title: One-way flow, and how we know
bullets: Air crosses the parabronchi back to front on both inhalation and exhalation
Flow probes in ducks (Bretz and Schmidt-Nielsen, 1971)
No valves: aerodynamic valving steers the air
Alligators have one-way flow too; theropod bones show air sacs
slides.notes: The “two breaths per parcel of air” rule is a useful summary, not a strict queue. The deep history links back to the dinosaur story in Chapter 1.

slides.title: Running hot
bullets: Core temperature about 38 to 42 °C; humans about 37 °C
Geese in a wind tunnel used energy about 16 times faster than at rest
In thin air, their flight metabolism fell rather than rose
Wild geese follow the terrain to save energy
slides.notes: Oxygen consumption is the standard measure of metabolic rate. Bird hearts are four-chambered and, on average, larger for body size than mammal hearts.

slides.title: Torpor and keeping cool
bullets: Small bodies lose heat fastest per gram
Hummingbirds use nightly torpor; one Andean species fell to about 3.3 °C
Common Poorwill: weeks of winter torpor
Cooling by panting and gular fluttering; countercurrent exchange in the legs
slides.notes: Work through the hummingbird and goose example. The size rule explains why torpor is most common in the smallest birds.

slides.title: From beak to cloaca
bullets: Beak: no teeth, food swallowed whole
Crop stores; pigeons make crop milk
Proventriculus: acid and enzymes
Gizzard grinds, often with grit
slides.notes: Use Figure 3.2. Each organ takes over part of the work that teeth and a single stomach do in a mammal.

slides.title: Guts that fit the life
bullets: Hoatzin: leaves fermented in the crop
Owl pellets of fur and bone
Godwits shrink their guts before a nonstop ocean crossing
Caudipteryx: stomach stones in a feathered dinosaur
slides.notes: Diet and travel both shape the gut. The godwit returns in Chapter 7 as our record-setting migrant.

slides.title: Seeing in four colors
bullets: Humans: three cone types; most birds: four
Fourth cone sensitive to violet or ultraviolet
Oil droplets sharpen color discrimination
Measured cell by cell with microspectrophotometry
slides.notes: Use Figure 3.3. Blue Tit crowns reflect ultraviolet, and males and females differ in ways we cannot see without instruments.

slides.title: Hearing and smell
bullets: Best hearing about 1 to 4 kHz; few birds hear above 10 kHz
Robins can find buried prey by sound
Barn Owls strike prey in total darkness
Turkey Vultures, kiwis and tubenoses hunt by smell
slides.notes: The old view that birds cannot smell was wrong. The vulture case study shows how to test a sense with a controlled experiment.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Air sacs give one-way airflow and efficient gas exchange
High body temperature is costly; torpor saves energy
Crop, proventriculus and gizzard replace teeth
Bird senses differ from ours: ultraviolet color, sharp hearing, and smell in some groups
slides.notes: Before the quiz, do the practice problems and try to explain the Bar-headed Goose’s flight in your own words, from air to muscle.

quiz.q: During exhalation, where does the air flowing through a bird’s parabronchi come from?
quiz.explanation: On exhalation the caudal sacs are squeezed and push the fresh air they received during inhalation forward through the parabronchi. The cranial sacs empty out through the trachea at the same time.

quiz.q: A physiologist finds that blood leaving a duck’s lung holds more oxygen than the air the duck breathes out. Which feature of the bird lung explains this?
choices: Gas exchange in the air sacs
quiz.explanation: In cross-current exchange, blood capillaries meet the air stream at many points, so the mixed blood can end up richer in oxygen than the exhaled air. Air sacs do little gas exchange, birds have no diaphragm, and bird lungs have no alveoli.

quiz.q: Which range of core body temperature is typical of most birds?
quiz.explanation: Most birds hold their core at about 38 to 42 °C, slightly higher when active. Humans are about 37 °C.

quiz.q: At dawn after a frosty night, a Ruby-throated Hummingbird is found perched motionless, fluffed up and slow to respond. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: It is asleep with a normal body temperature
It is in torpor and will rewarm by shivering
quiz.explanation: Hummingbirds lose heat quickly because they are so small, and they often enter torpor on cold nights, lowering body temperature and metabolic rate. They rewarm by shivering.

quiz.q: Which part of the digestive tract secretes acid and digestive enzymes?
quiz.explanation: The proventriculus is the glandular front part of the stomach. The crop stores food, the gizzard grinds it and the cloaca is the shared exit.

quiz.q: A newly described bird species lives on hard, dry seeds. Which feature would you predict in its gut?
choices: A thin gizzard with no grit
A thick, muscular gizzard containing grit
quiz.explanation: Hard seeds need grinding, so seed-eaters have thick, muscular gizzards and swallow grit. Thin gizzards go with soft foods such as fish, nectar or ripe fruit.

quiz.q: Petrels at sea fly toward a patch of water where researchers have released dimethyl sulfide. What does this suggest?
choices: They see ultraviolet light reflected from the patch
They follow the magnetic field to it
They use smell to find a compound linked to rich feeding areas
quiz.explanation: Dimethyl sulfide is released when small animals graze on plankton, so it marks productive water. Tubenoses such as petrels have a keen sense of smell and follow it.

quiz.q: How many types of single cone do most birds have?
quiz.explanation: Most birds have four single-cone types, one of them sensitive to violet or ultraviolet light, which makes their color vision tetrachromatic. Humans have three.

challenge.title: How a Bar-headed Goose crosses the Himalayas
challenge.prompt: Explain how a Bar-headed Goose can fly over the Himalayas. Trace oxygen from the thin mountain air to the goose’s flight muscles, naming each step in the respiratory and circulatory systems, and say where the goose differs from a lowland bird. Then explain how its flight behavior (route, time of day and altitude) reduces the demand on that system. Finish by correcting the popular claim that these geese fly over the summit of Everest, using the tracking evidence.
challenge.deliverable: A written explanation of 300 to 500 words, with an optional labeled sketch of the oxygen pathway from air sac to muscle.
rubric: Describes the air sacs, one-way airflow through the parabronchi and cross-current exchange correctly
Names at least two goose specializations, such as deeper breathing, hemoglobin that binds oxygen more tightly or more capillaries in the flight muscles, and explains what each does
Uses the tracking and wind-tunnel evidence: terrain-following flight, most flight below 6,000 meters, and lower flight metabolism in thin air
Corrects the Everest claim with the 7,290-meter maximum and explains that the birds follow valleys and passes

challenge.title: Watch a bird eat
challenge.prompt: Spend 20 minutes watching one bird feed: an American Robin on a lawn, pigeons in a park, or birds at a feeder. Record every behavior that tells you something about its senses or its digestion, such as head tilts, swallowing food whole, a bulging crop, pecking at grit or droppings. For each one, name the structure or sense from this chapter that is at work, and say what you could not tell from watching alone.
challenge.deliverable: Field notes with the date, place, species and times of each observation, followed by one paragraph of 100 to 200 words interpreting what you saw.
rubric: Identifies the species and records at least five dated, specific observations
Links each observation correctly to a structure or sense from this chapter
Distinguishes what was observed from what was inferred
Proposes at least one way an experiment could test an inference, as in the robin and vulture examples

corrections.before: Turkey Vultures find hidden carcasses by odor, kiwis sniff for worms through nostrils at the tip of the bill, and tubenoses track the smell of dimethyl sulfide across the ocean.
corrections.after: Turkey Vultures find hidden carcasses by odor, kiwis sniff for worms through nostrils at the tip of the bill, and many tubenoses track the smell of dimethyl sulfide across the ocean.
corrections.why: Attraction to DMS varies among tubenose species (Nevitt et al. 1995), so the statement should not cover the whole group.

review.summary: The chapter is accurate overall: all 19 section sources are real and correctly cited, the airflow figure and the breath-order interactive show the correct two-cycle, back-to-front route, the figure 3 cone peaks match published values (Blue Tit about 372/449/502/563 nm per Hart et al. 2000; human about 420/530/560 nm), and every multiple-choice key is correct. The corrections are refinements, not reversals: they narrow overgeneralizations (DMS attraction across all tubenoses, colored oil droplets in every cone, crops in 'most birds of prey', pigeon ceca), describe the godwit sample correctly, and soften one unverified percentage.
